The Box That Runs the Show: What a Hybrid Inverter Actually Does

Panels make the power. The inverter decides where it goes. Here's how to read the spec sheet.

Rick O'Shay Solar

Panels get all the attention. They're the part you see from the road. But the box on the wall is the one making the decisions: where the power goes, when the battery charges, and what happens the second the grid drops out. That box is the inverter, and on a solar-plus-storage system it's usually a hybrid inverter.

Here's what it does, and how to read the spec sheet without a decoder ring.

Inverter 101: DC In, AC Out

The U.S. Department of Energy calls the inverter one of the most important pieces of equipment in a solar energy system. Solar panels make direct current (DC). Your house and the grid run on alternating current (AC). The inverter converts one to the other by switching the DC input back and forth very rapidly, then cleaning it up into a smooth sine wave.

DOE also notes that a household inverter usually does more than convert power. It can monitor the system and talk to the internet, and solar-plus-battery systems rely on advanced inverters to run without support from the grid during an outage, if they're designed to do so.

That last part is the "hybrid" job. A hybrid inverter manages three things at once: the solar array, a battery bank, and the grid (plus, often, a generator).

Reading a Real Spec Sheet: The Sol-Ark 15K

Sol-Ark is one of the inverter brands Accutek Solar works with, so let's use its 15K whole-home hybrid inverter as the example. These numbers are from Sol-Ark's June 2025 datasheet (Rev. 5):

  • 15,000 W nominal real power at 240V when running on solar and batteries together.
  • 12,000 W continuous off-grid from batteries alone, with 13,000 W for up to 30 minutes and 24,000 W for 10 seconds. That short-term surge matters because, as Kohler explains, a motor's starting current is typically six times its rated full-load current.
  • 5 ms backup transfer time. That's 5 thousandths of a second to switch to backup when the grid goes down.
  • 200 A grid pass-through. Grid power can flow through the inverter to your loads at up to 200 amps.
  • Three MPPTs with two strings each, and up to 19,500 W of usable PV power.
  • 48V battery input with up to 275 A charge and discharge current.
  • Built-in automatic generator start (2-wire) and a dedicated generator port.
  • IP65 / NEMA 3R enclosure and a 10-year standard warranty.

Editor's note, Oct. 2026: Sol-Ark issued a revised datasheet (Rev. 8) on Sept. 10, 2026. Every number in the list above is unchanged on it. A few other specs did change between versions, including the rated MPPT operating voltage range, the battery operating voltage range, the listed height and the grid-to-battery charge efficiency, so we left those out. Always design from the manufacturer's current sheet.

What Those Numbers Mean at Your House

MPPT stands for maximum power point tracking. The PVsyst design software documentation notes that multiple MPPT inputs can work as semi-independent inverters. In practice, that's what lets one inverter take panel groups that don't match, like a south roof and a ground mount out back.

Continuous vs. surge is the difference between what the inverter can run all day and what it can deliver for a moment. Both matter when you're planning backup for a farmhouse with a well, a freezer and a shop compressor.

Pass-through current matters because the inverter sits between the grid and your loads. A high pass-through rating lets it handle a full household's grid power when the sun's down and the battery is resting.

Generator start means the inverter can signal a standby generator to kick on, for example during a long outage, so solar, battery and generator work as one system. If you already own a Kohler, that's a conversation worth having.

One Inverter Doesn't Fit Every Home

The 15K is built for whole-home backup. Plenty of homes need less, and some need two units in parallel. Sol-Ark lists the 15K as stackable up to 12 units. The right pick depends on your loads, your battery plans and how much of the house you want running in an outage. Accutek Solar also installs Victron Energy, OutBack Power, Solis, Fronius and other brands, and the right one depends on the job.
